cands.name: Joe Males

money.note: Individuals gave $1,055,962; PAC money $1,450; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Marine Corps veteran (honorably discharged as a Sergeant) and owner of a computer networking services business he started in 1996. Serves on the Hemet City Council. Ran as the Republican nominee for California's 25th Congressional District in 2026.

endorsements.text: Endorsed by the Republican Party of California, per Ballotpedia, along with voter-guide recommendations from April's Common Sense Cali Voters, Elizabeth Barcohana's Lady with a Brain Voter Guide, and The Morning Answer with Jennifer Horn.

His campaign site lists endorsements from Assemblymen Jeff Gonzalez and Greg Wallis, mayors of Needles, Temecula, San Jacinto and Hemet, other local council members and water and school board members, the California Republican Party, the Republican Parties of Riverside and San Bernardino counties, and the California Republican Assembly.

cands.gaps: We could not find where Joe Males was born or raised, or when he came to California. We found no stated positions or actions on data centers, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, growth and land protection, H-1B and immigration enforcement, policing, gun policy, abortion, or school choice and teacher pay. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey, and his campaign site gives only a general biography. His time on the Hemet City Council is described only on his own campaign site, and we found no independent record of the dates he served or of specific council votes. We found no reporting on controversies.

cands.bio: Physician and Democratic U.S. representative from California, serving since 2013 (District 36, then District 25 since the 2022 redistricting). Former emergency physician at Eisenhower Medical Center and senior associate dean at UC Riverside School of Medicine. Holds an M.D. and two other graduate degrees from Harvard.

controversies.text: Federal records show $22,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $11,808 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26.
Missed 8 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (1.2%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 2, 2025-01-07 to 2025-01-09.

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include the Democratic Party of California, California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), California Teachers Association, California Environmental Voters and Equality California.

cands.gaps: We found no stated positions or official actions from Ruiz on statewide data-center bans, data-center or development rezonings, homestead property tax relief, limits on investor or foreign land buying, gun laws, abortion, or school choice. We found nothing on police pay or pensions, and nothing on H-1B visas beyond the immigration votes listed. He did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey in any recent cycle. His campaign site describes priorities such as Medicare, Social Security, veterans, the Salton Sea and healthcare, but these do not address the issues above. The year he moved to Coachella and his age at the time are not given in the pages reviewed. The Ballotpedia page was cut off partway through the 117th Congress key votes, so earlier votes were not read.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.
